Single-target GLP-1 receptor agonism plateaus in a recognizable pattern: benefit is most reliable for steatosis and inflammation, more inconsistent for advanced fibrosis, and prone to erosion after treatment withdrawal. Zhou and Dong [@Zhou2026From] frame this as a structural limitation rather than simply insufficient potency — GLP-1R-based therapies act predominantly through indirect, systemic metabolic regulation, so their efficacy is bounded by the integrity of intrahepatic and systemic signaling networks, the severity of baseline metabolic derangement, and the persistence of drug exposure. Multi-receptor agonists are positioned as a direct response to this ceiling, expanding regulatory input by co-activating the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor (GIPR) and, in newer molecules, the glucagon receptor (GCGR) alongside GLP-1R.

Tirzepatide, the first approved dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist, illustrates this expanded mechanism in clinical practice. As a multi-organ integrator, it raises insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon, slows gastric emptying, and produces weight loss substantially greater than GLP-1 monoagonism, with downstream effects on adipose tissue, gut microbiota composition, and intestinal barrier integrity that plausibly reinforce its hepatic actions [@Khan2026Tirzepatide]. The clearest imaging evidence for a hepatic effect independent of glycemic control comes from the SURPASS-3 MRI substudy, in which tirzepatide significantly reduced MRI-assessed liver fat content compared with insulin degludec in insulin-naïve patients with type 2 diabetes and MASLD [@Cusi2026Liver]. A post hoc analysis of that substudy tested whether this benefit depended on genetic steatosis risk, comparing liver fat and cardiometabolic changes at 52 weeks by presence (GG/CG) or absence (CC) of the PNPLA3 I148M variant; tirzepatide-treated participants showed significant reductions in liver fat content, weight, and HbA1c regardless of genotype, suggesting the drug's hepatic effect is not contingent on a specific lipogenic risk allele [@Cusi2026Liver]. The SYNERGY-NASH trial extends this signal to histology, with tirzepatide achieving MASH resolution in 44%-62% of patients versus 10% on placebo and fibrosis improvement in up to 51% versus 30% [@Amorim2026GLP].

Real-world data reinforce the trial findings while adding mechanistic texture. In a retrospective multicenter study of 23 adults with obesity and MASLD (fatty liver index [FLI] > 44) treated with tirzepatide 2.5-5 mg weekly for three months, body weight, BMI, waist circumference, fasting glucose, HbA1c, HOMA-IR, hs-CRP, liver enzymes, and FLI all declined significantly (p < 0.001 for most comparisons) [@Galasso2026Tirzepatide]. Change in FLI correlated with change in weight, BMI, waist circumference, hs-CRP, HbA1c, AST, and HDL cholesterol, but on multiple regression only ΔC-reactive protein remained an independent predictor of ΔFLI, explaining 29.8% of the variance — implicating reduced low-grade inflammation, not weight loss alone, as a driver of hepatic improvement [@Galasso2026Tirzepatide]. A complementary question — whether switching from an existing GLP-1RA to tirzepatide adds incremental hepatic benefit — was addressed by the Hokkaido-TZP study, a retrospective secondary analysis of 182 patients with type 2 diabetes at high MASLD risk who converted from GLP-1RA therapy to tirzepatide [@Takiyama2026Clinical]. Over six months, switching reduced HbA1c, body weight, and liver enzymes, and lowered the Hepatic Steatosis Index in both fibrosis-risk strata; critically, a significant reduction in FIB-4 index emerged only in the high fibrosis-risk group (P < 0.001), and this improvement was not correlated with change in BMI or HbA1c — baseline HSI instead correlated with the magnitude of FIB-4 change (ρ = 0.234, P = 0.005) [@Takiyama2026Clinical]. Together these two studies suggest tirzepatide's fibrosis-related benefit is partly dissociated from its weight and glycemic effects, consistent with a genuinely broader receptor-level mechanism rather than a more potent version of the same GLP-1 pathway.

Beyond tirzepatide, a growing evidence base now speaks to dual and triple GLP-1-based polyagonists as a class. A systematic review and meta-analysis pooling six randomized trials (961 participants) of tirzepatide, survodutide, pemvidutide, retatrutide, and cotadutide against placebo found that polyagonist therapy significantly increased MASH resolution or histological improvement without fibrosis worsening (RR 3.32, 95% CI 2.28-4.84; I² = 20%) and fibrosis improvement without MASH worsening (RR 1.49, 95% CI 1.15-1.94; I² = 0%), alongside a much larger relative reduction in liver fat content than has typically been reported for GLP-1 monotherapy (MD -44.60 percentage points, 95% CI -51.17 to -38.04) and a markedly increased likelihood of achieving at least a 30% relative reduction in MRI-PDFF (RR 4.71, 95% CI 3.04-7.30) [@Santos2026Efficacy]. Gastrointestinal adverse events (nausea, diarrhea, vomiting) were more frequent with polyagonists, though serious adverse events and treatment discontinuation did not differ significantly from placebo [@Santos2026Efficacy]. A network meta-analysis incorporating these newer agents alongside SGLT2 inhibitors and FGF21 analogs across 34 studies ranked GLP-1/GIP dual agonists highest of all drug classes for MASH resolution (RR 5.21), ahead of FGF21 analogs (RR 3.52) and SGLT2 inhibitors (RR 2.92); FGF21 analogs and SGLT2 inhibitors instead led on fibrosis improvement specifically (RR 2.22 and RR 2.27, respectively), with GLP-1 monoagonists trailing (RR 1.51) [@Tang2026Updating]. This dissociation — polyagonists excelling at inflammatory/histological resolution, other mechanisms edging ahead on fibrosis regression — underscores that "beyond GLP-1" does not yet mean a single agent dominates every histological endpoint.

Glucagon receptor co-agonism introduces a distinct cardiovascular consideration not present with GIP co-agonism. Because glucagon regulates energy expenditure and lipid metabolism in addition to glucose homeostasis, GCGR/GLP-1 dual agonists such as mazdutide and survodutide were designed to extend metabolic benefit, but exogenous glucagon also has acute chronotropic, inotropic, and hypertensive effects, raising a theoretical safety question even though unequivocal evidence of GCGR expression in human myocardium is lacking [@Kushner2026Cardiovascular]. In clinical studies, mazdutide and survodutide increased heart rate to an extent similar to GLP-1 monoagonists — a class already considered cardioprotective despite this chronotropic effect — while also lowering blood pressure and improving hyperglycemia; however, at least one other GCGR/GLP-1 dual agonist was discontinued in development partly because of unacceptably large heart-rate increases and QT-interval prolongation, a difference the authors attribute to varying relative potency at the two receptors [@Kushner2026Cardiovascular]. Dedicated cardiovascular outcomes data are still pending, notably the SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT trial evaluating survodutide and a companion thorough QT study, meaning glucagon receptor co-agonism carries real, compound-specific cardiovascular uncertainty that GIP co-agonism does not [@Kushner2026Cardiovascular].

Taken together, this evidence supports dual and, increasingly, triple agonism as the mechanistic strategy most likely to close the gap between MASLD's inflammatory and fibrotic components — with dual GLP-1/GIP agonism already showing superior metabolic control and steatosis reduction, even as definitive histological confirmation of fibrosis reversal remains incomplete for several agents in the class [@Chianetta2026Emerging]. Broader incretin-class meta-analyses (24 RCTs, n = 2158) confirm consistent reductions in ALT, AST, and liver fat relative to placebo and insulin, but note that effects on histologic fibrosis remain inconclusive across the incretin category as a whole, reinforcing that fibrosis resolution — not steatosis or inflammation — is where the efficacy ceiling of GLP-1-based therapy, single or multi-receptor, is still most evident [@Tesoro2026Impact]. Whether multi-receptor agonism can also address the hardest population — compensated MASH-related cirrhosis — remains unresolved: GLP-1R/GCGR dual agonists are among the agents now being tested in this setting, but the predominance of negative trials for cirrhosis-stage disease suggests that receptor expansion alone may not overcome the added burden of stabilized fibrosis, portal hypertension, and patient heterogeneity that characterizes advanced disease [@Zeng2026Drug].
